summary.summary: Wigan's year-end treasury review shows a compliant but growing debt book: loan debt rose £52.2m to £440.2m in 2025/26 (£67m of new loans at 4.34%-4.74%), against a borrowing need (CFR) of £623.3m, leaving the council £137.2m under-borrowed — running on internal cash rather than external debt. Treasury investments rose to £43.2m earning 5.17%, and all borrowing stayed inside the £678.7m authorised limit. The new borrowing was deliberately short-dated (all four 2025/26 loans mature by June 2027) to avoid locking in long-term rates above 5%, so the council returns to the market to refinance from late 2026 onward.

signals.headline: Loan debt up £52.2m to £440.2m in 2025/26; £67m of new loans taken at 4.34%-4.74%
signals.why: Wigan is steadily externalising a borrowing need that still sits £137m above its external debt, making it a recurring borrower.

signals.headline: £101.5m of PWLB debt matures within 24 months of 31 March 2026 (£26.2m under 12 months, £75.3m in 12-24 months), plus the £20m and £37m 2025/26 loans falling due Oct 2026-Jun 2027
signals.why: The deliberate short-dating strategy defers rate risk rather than removing it — this debt rolls over at whatever rates prevail from late 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Wigan's schools deficit for children with special needs stands at £25.9m, with £2.6m left for the council to fund
news_drafts.lead:
Wigan Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) stood at £25.934m on 31 March 2026, according to its medium-term financial plan (the council's plan for the next three years). The cabinet paper puts the cause as a £34.028m cumulative overspend on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

Government will award a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the deficit, about £23.3m. That leaves £2.593m for Wigan Council to fund. The paper says the government has not confirmed further support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, and the council estimates about £3.5m of additional liability across those two years. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off the council's main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028. After that, the paper says, any unfunded schools deficit becomes a core budget issue.

The high needs overspend is projected to continue: £17.547m in 2026/27 and £17.979m in 2027/28. The paper attributes it to rising numbers and complexity of pupils at maintained special schools, growth in education, health and care plans (EHCPs), high-cost independent school places outside the borough, and post-16 provision. These are recurring annual overspends, not one-off pressures. The council is implementing an Inclusion and SEND Strategic Plan, though the paper says its full impact will take time.

news_drafts.headline: Wigan cuts capital spending by £49m as major building projects face delays
news_drafts.lead: Wigan Council has reduced its capital programme by £48.78m, about a fifth of its planned spending, due to widespread delays across major schemes including schools, housing, and town centre regeneration. The 2026/27 budget was revised from £239.5m to £190.7m, with slippages in projects such as Haigh Hall (£11.1m rephased to 2028/29), Hope School relocation (£9.9m) and Wood Fold school (£5.3m), reflecting constraints from re-procurement, planning processes and pending external funding approvals. The council is undertaking a three-year capital programme totalling £464.6m to 2028/29, heavily reliant on prudential borrowing — money a council borrows against future income — with the town centre regeneration framework alone requiring £96.4m in new debt. Spending is heavily concentrated in 2026/27, placing substantial cash-flow demands on the coming year.

findings.headline: General Fund balances being rebuilt with £2.5m added in 2026/27 and £1m annual contributions planned 2027/28 onwards, but still modest relative to budget gaps.
findings.detail: Council transferred £2.5m into General Fund balances in 2026/27 and plans further £1m annual contributions. This is intended to strengthen resilience and capacity to manage emerging risks. Earmarked reserves estimated at £58.9m at 31 March 2027. Use of reserves for one-off expenditure reduced significantly in 2025/26, reflecting commitment to sustainable reserve levels. However, reserve building remains modest relative to £8.5m–£18.9m annual savings requirements.
findings.matters: Deliberate attempt to strengthen financial resilience, but constrained by budget gaps; shows management discipline but relative insufficiency.
findings.figures: £2.5m transferred 2026/27; £1m planned annual contributions 2027/28 onwards; £58.9m earmarked reserves at 31 March 2027
findings.quote: the Council transferred £2.5m into General Fund balances during 2026/27 and plans to make further contributions of £1m in 2027/28 and subsequent years.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income of £6m per annum expected to reduce as packaging sector adapts; Deposit Return Scheme (October 2027) will further reduce recycling income.
findings.detail: EPR scheme currently yields council £6m annually. As producers respond to EPR requirements through packaging reduction and substitution, this income stream is forecast to decline (amount unquantified). Separately, Deposit Return Scheme commencing October 2027 will remove valuable drinks containers from local authority recycling streams, reducing income further and increasing processing costs. Council has also accelerated collection of flexible plastics (April 2026), though national mandate was postponed to 2030.
findings.matters: Material income source at risk; compound effect of two policy changes reducing recycling income and increasing costs; forecast impact on budget not yet quantified.
findings.figures: £6m per annum from EPR (at risk); DRS commencing October 2027
findings.quote: Presently under this scheme we receive around £6m per annum for dealing with this waste. This may reduce as the sector responds to the changes.

findings.headline: Maintained mainstream schools' financial position deteriorated, with 50 of 86 schools in in-year deficit and 11 in cumulative deficit in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Schools' aggregate balances fell £0.669m in 2025/26 despite being the largest sector. Falling pupil numbers (149 fewer primary, 76 fewer secondary in October 2025 census) will reduce funding allocations further. Council is providing support to schools in cumulative deficit, but sector-wide pressure is evident and structural (not cyclical), given demographic decline.
findings.matters: Delegated budget sector in stress; indicates schools cannot absorb cost pressures; falling pupil numbers are structural not temporary; potential for growing council support requirement.
findings.figures: 50 of 86 schools in in-year deficit; 11 in cumulative deficit; balances down £0.669m in 2025/26; 149 fewer primary pupils, 76 fewer secondary pupils in October 2025 census
findings.quote: In 2025/26 Maintained mainstream schools' balances reduced by £0.669m, with 50 of the 86 schools reporting in-year deficits.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review delivered lower funding growth to Wigan than comparable authorities; Business Rates Retention reset redistributed 13 years of accumulated growth.
findings.detail: The December 2025 Fair Funding Review reassessed resource allocation across councils using updated needs assessment. Wigan's outcome was lower funding growth than many peers, reflecting lower relative needs assessment. Business Rates Retention Scheme was reset for the first time since April 2013; accumulated business rates growth since 2013 was redistributed to other councils in line with new assessment. This is a structural change in Wigan's funding trajectory relative to peers.
findings.matters: Structural weakening of Wigan's funding position relative to comparators; limits council's flexibility versus peer councils; no recovery mechanism.
findings.figures: Lower funding growth than comparable authorities (specific differential not disclosed); business rates reset after 13 years of retention.
findings.quote: the revised funding arrangements have resulted in Wigan receiving a lower level of funding growth than many comparable authorities.

findings.headline: High Needs Block projected to overspend £17.5m (2026/27) and £17.9m (2027/28), driven by EHCP growth and out-of-borough independent school placements.
findings.detail: High Needs overspend is driven by rising numbers and complexity of pupils at maintained special schools, EHCP growth, high-cost out-of-borough independent school placements, and post-16 SEND. The council is implementing an Inclusion and SEND Strategic Plan, but full impact will take time. These are recurring annual overspends, not one-off pressures.
findings.matters: Ongoing structural overspend; indicates capacity and pricing challenge in SEND provision; feeds DSG deficit tracked separately but will merge into General Fund post-2028.
findings.quote: The current projection is for an overspend in 26/27 of £17.547m and an overspend of £17.979m in 27/28.
